[[Dulles, Virginia]], United States | coordinates = {{WikidataCoord|Q136544402|region:US-VA_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | years_built = | groundbreaking_date = | start_date = April 1960 | stop_date = | completion_date = | opened_date = November 17, 1962 | inauguration_date = | demolition_date = | architect = [[Eero Saarinen]] | owner = | cost = | floor_area = {{cvt|1.1|e6ft2}} | floor_count = 2 (+2 basement) | parking = | public_transit = | references = | architectural_style = [[Mid-century modern]] | height = | architecture_firm = | structural_engineer = [[Ammann & Whitney]] | services_engineer = [[Burns & McDonnell]] (mechanical) | main_contractor = Corbetta Construction Company | ren_architect = [[Skidmore, Owings and Merrill]] | renovation_date = 1978–1980, 1993–1996, 2000–2010 | closing_date = | topped_out_date = | relocated_date = | material = Glass, metal, concrete | size = | website = }} The '''Dulles International Airport Main Terminal''' is located in [[Loudoun County, Virginia|Loudoun]] and [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax counties]] in [[Dulles, Virginia]], United States. The original structure, {{Convert|600|ft}} long and {{Convert|150|ft}} wide, was designed by [[Eero Saarinen]] and completed in 1962 as the first terminal at [[Dulles International Airport]]. Annexes to the west and east were completed in 1996 as part of a renovation designed by [[Skidmore, Owings & Merrill]] (SOM), bringing its total length to {{Convert|1240|ft}}. The terminal is operated by the [[Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority]], which operates Dulles Airport as a whole. The terminal's design is a [[suspended structure]] with roof panels of precast concrete suspended between cables which span the width of the building. The Main Terminal's design includes parallel slanted [[colonnade]]s on the terminal's north and south facades, interspersed with glass walls. The [[landside]] facade to the north is taller than the [[airside]] facade to the south; a concave roof supported by cables connects the two facades, descending toward the center. A concourse and [[control tower]] extend south toward the airport's [[Airport apron|apron]]. The interior was originally divided into two levels: an upper story for departing passengers and a lower story for arriving passengers. Saarinen's original design included [[mobile lounge]]s that ferried passengers directly to planes, reducing the need for long walks or [[taxiing]] while increasing the airport's operational flexibility. The modern terminal includes four [[Gate (airport)|airline gates]] known as Z gates, where aircraft could unload passengers directly. In addition, two basements contain security screening facilities and an [[AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)|AeroTrain]] people-mover station. The 1950 Washington Airport Act provided funding for Dulles Airport, land for which was acquired in January 1958. Saarinen was selected that May to design the terminal, construction of which began in early 1960. After several delays, the terminal was dedicated on November 17, 1962, along with the rest of the airport. Initially, Dulles Airport saw lower-than-expected usage, but increased patronage prompted the airport's original operator, the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] (FAA), to contemplate an expansion in the early 1970s. [[HOK (firm)|Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum]] (HOK) built two small annexes to the south in 1978, and further expansions and additional terminals were contemplated in the 1980s following increases in patronage. SOM designed annexes to the west and east, which began construction in October 1993 and were dedicated on September 6, 1996. Additional expansions took place in the 2000s, including the Z gates and the basements. The structure was widely acclaimed when it was completed, particularly regarding its shape; Saarinen reportedly considered it his best work. The terminal has received numerous awards, including the [[American Institute of Architects]]' [[Twenty-five Year Award]], and other terminal buildings have been compared with it. Though the Main Terminal was nominated for inclusion on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 1978, it was never added due to objections from the FAA. ==Description== The Main Terminal of [[Dulles International Airport]] is in [[Dulles, Virginia]], United States, some {{Convert|26|to|27|mi}} from Washington, D.C.{{cite web |last=Haughland |first=Vern |date=December 17, 1962 |title=New Dulles Airport Making Hit with Public |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-nonpareil-new-dulles-airport-m/182870928/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Daily Nonpareil |page=12 |agency=Associated Press }}{{Cite news |date=November 18, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport Dedicated by Kennedy, Ike |work=Boston Globe |page=27 |id={{ProQuest|276440147}} }}{{Efn|The airport is so large that both of these figures are correct, depending on where the distance is being measured from. However, some figures give a substantially different (and incorrect) figure of {{Convert|17|mi}}.{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|page=245|ps=. }}}} The airport, serving the [[Washington metropolitan area]], straddles the border between [[Loudoun County, Virginia|Loudoun]] and [[Fairfax County, Virginia|Fairfax counties]].{{cite web |last=Yarbrough |first=Charles |date=July 22, 1960 |title=Scenic Road to Shorten Ride to Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-scenic-road-to-shorten-ride/182917742/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Evening Star |page=19 }} The terminal is placed between Dulles Airport's original north–south runways.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=January 31, 1960 |title=Design of Dulles Airport Is Futuristic as Jet Age: Sphere Atop Control Tower |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141111328}} }}{{harvnb|Stroud|1980|ps=.|page=558 }} It is one of several terminal structures at Dulles Airport, along with several outlying "midfield concourses" and the International Arrivals Building,{{cite web |date=November 17, 1962 |title=Airport Overview |url=https://www.flydulles.com/airport-overview |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=flydulles.com }}{{harvnb|Mehaffy|2005|ps=.|page=S5 }} all of which were developed after the original terminal.{{cite web |year=2010 |title=Facts About Washington Dulles International Airport |url=http://www.mwaa.com/dulles/663.htm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130129064433/http://www.mwaa.com/dulles/663.htm |archive-date=January 29, 2013 |access-date=October 12, 2010 |publisher=Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority }} The terminal was built to smaller dimensions than comparable terminals at other airports because it used [[mobile lounge]]s, which transported passengers from the terminal to planes{{cite web |last=McLeod |first=John F. |date=April 8, 1959 |title=Chantilly Maps 'Mobile Lounge' |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-washington-daily-news-chantilly-maps/182906709/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Washington Daily News |pages=7, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-washington-daily-news-chantilly-maps/182906773/ 53] }}{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|page=219|ps=. }}{{cite web |last=Armstrong |first=Sam B. |date=January 31, 1960 |title=Dulles International Is Example of New Concept in Airport Design |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch-dulles-internati/182932626/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |page=19 }} and, later, to the concourses. The original terminal was designed in a [[mid-century modern]] style by [[Eero Saarinen]]{{cite book |last=American Institute of Architects |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mPJPAAAAMAAJ |title=Mid-century Architecture in America: Honor Awards of the American Institute of Architects, 1949–1961 |date=1961 |publisher=Johns Hopkins Press |page=243 }}{{cite book |author=DK |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=FlLYEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA320 |title=Architecture: The Definitive Visual Guide |publisher=DK |year=2023 |isbn=978-0-593-84590-5 |series=DK Definitive Cultural Histories |page=320 |access-date=October 21, 2025 }} and was his only work in Virginia.{{cite web |last=Young |first=Julie |date=October 24, 2008 |title=Modern look rounds out old style |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-modern-look-roun/183357258/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=D6 }} Saarinen worked with structural engineering firm [[Ammann & Whitney]], mechanical engineering firm [[Burns & McDonnell]], and airport consultant Charles Landrum.{{harvnb|Architectural Forum|1963|ps=.|page=82 }} The Corbetta Construction Company was the main contractor, while Humphreys & Harding installed the finishes. Other figures involved in the building's construction included lighting consultant [[Richard Kelly (lighting designer)|Richard Kelly]] and landscape designer [[Dan Kiley]]. The Main Terminal was intended to symbolize the [[Jet Age]]{{harvnb|Román|2003|page=117|ps=. }} and, from the outset, was designed with future expansions in mind.{{cite magazine |last=Greer |first=Nora Richter |date=May 1988 |title=Eero Saarinen's Dulles Airport Wins AIA 21-Year Award |url=https://www.usmodernist.org/AJ/A-1988-05.pdf |magazine=Architecture: the AIA Journal |pages=38, 43 }} Saarinen described his design as a "huge continuous hammock suspended between concrete trees", saying it represented a solution for what to put "between earth and sky". The western and eastern annexes were designed by [[David Childs]], Michael McCarthy, and Marilyn Taylor of [[Skidmore, Owings and Merrill]] (SOM) in a similar style to the original building.{{Harvnb|Baneneche|1993|ps=.|page=40 }} Ammann & Whitney was also the engineer for SOM's expansion. === Exterior === [[File:Airport_Washington_Dulles_05.jpg|thumb|View from the south (2020)]] The original terminal measured {{Convert|600|ft}} long and {{Convert|150|ft}} wide.{{Cite news |last=Jones |first=Alfred |date=June 10, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport—Where You 'Ferry' To Plane: Mobile Lounges To Carry Passengers From Terminal To Jets At New Airfield |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=FA1 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|542421695}} }}{{Efn|Other sources give a width of {{Convert|152|ft}} or {{Convert|200|ft}}.}} Both ends were built with provisions for extensions measuring {{Convert|300|ft|-1}} long,{{Efn|Other sources say the building was constructed with provisions for extensions measuring {{Convert|320|ft|m}} long. giving the terminal an ultimate length of {{Convert|1240|ft}}.}} for a total length of {{Convert|1200|ft}}.{{cite web |date=February 17, 1960 |title=Plans Unveiled for Capital's Dulles International Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-plans-unveiled-for-capitals-d/182909718/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Times |page=69 }}{{cite web |last=Kenworthy |first=E. W. |date=November 18, 1962 |title=Kennedy and Eisenhower Hail New Dulles Airport |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/11/18/archives/kennedy-and-eisenhower-hail-new-dulles-airport-2-leaders-hail.html |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The base of the original terminal, including vehicular ramps, was intended to support such an expansion,{{cite book |last1=Ames |first1=D.L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SoaXrA21G8sC&pg=PA190 |title=Design & Historic Preservation: The Challenge of Compatibility : Held at Goucher College, Baltimore, Maryland, March 14–16, 2002 |last2=Wagner |first2=R.D. |author3=Goucher College |publisher=University of Delaware Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-87413-831-3 |page=190 }}{{harvnb|Freeman|1997|page=67|ps=. }} which was intended to have the same cross-section as the original terminal.{{cite news |last=Lewis |first=Roger K. |date=March 26, 1994 |title=Dulles Needs To Spread Its Wings |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/realestate/1994/03/26/dulles-needs-to-spread-its-wings/0dbf87ec-901e-460d-8865-b8eac7bc92e9/ |access-date=October 19, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=E1 |id={{ProQuest|750973850}} }} In particular, the vehicular ramps paralleled the terminal for its entire proposed length, and Saarinen added empty openings at the terminal's base to accommodate future entrances. When the annexes were eventually built in the 1990s, they were {{Convert|320|ft}} long,{{Cite magazine |last=Reingold |first=Lester |date=Apr 1994 |title=Capital improvements |magazine=Air Transport World |page=46 |volume=31 |issue=4 |id={{ProQuest|224298137}} }}{{Cite magazine |last1=Cullerton |first1=Richard |last2=Gravallese |first2=Albert J. |date=Apr 1996 |title=Capital facelift takes flight |magazine=Civil Engineering |page=40 |volume=66 |issue=4 |id={{ProQuest|228490475}} }}{{cite web |date=November 17, 1996 |title=Washington Spiffing Up Its Two Airports |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-times-tribune-washington-spiffing-up/183347960/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=The Times-Tribune |page=97 }} giving the terminal a total length of {{Convert|1240|ft}}.{{cite news |last=Reid |first=Alice |date=September 6, 1996 |title=Additional Space a Cause For Celebration at Dulles; New Wings at Main Terminal Are Dedicated |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B.05 |id={{ProQuest|307934269}} }} Just west of the Main Terminal is the International Arrivals Terminal, which abuts the Main Terminal's base. The vehicular drop-off and pick-up ramps are on the north, or [[landside]], facade of the terminal; there were originally separate loading bays for taxis, private vehicles, and buses or limousines.{{cite web |last=Ashton |first=Betty Parker |date=September 24, 1961 |title=Dulles Airport Near Chantilly To Be Largest |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-dulles-airport-n/182930618/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |pages=F1, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-dulles-airport-n/182930636/ F13] }} The ramps loop around a parking area nicknamed the "bowl",{{cite news |last=Sipress |first=Alan |date=September 12, 1998 |title=Prowling for Parking; New Spaces Don't Meet Demand, but Dulles Plans Thousands More |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B01 |id={{ProQuest|408414050}} }} while later parking garages were built away from the terminal to preserve views of the building.{{cite magazine |date=Sep 2000 |title=Dulles Airport launches $3.2-billion capital plan |magazine=Civil Engineering |page=28 |volume=70 |issue=9 |id={{ProQuest|228439020}} }} The ramps are reached by the [[Dulles Access Road]], which leads east toward Washington, D.C.{{cite news |last=Kohlmeier |first=Louis M. |date=November 16, 1962 |title=New Dulles Airport Provokes Washington Debate on Its Merits: Mobile Lounges, New Radar Hailed by FAA; Critics Call Field Costly White Elephant New Dulles Airport Provokes Washington Debate on Its Merits |work=The Wall Street Journal |page=1 |issn=0099-9660 |id={{ProQuest|132732974}} }} The Dulles Access Road, the airport's original main approach road, was intended as a major part of the terminal's design, providing passengers views of the building as it emerged from the landscape;{{harvnb|Mehaffy|2005|ps=.|page=4.8 }} it was landscaped by Kiley.{{harvnb|Freeman|1997|page=63|ps=. }} Plans for a [[Washington Metro]] line to serve the terminal had been considered since the 1960s,{{Cite news |last=Eisen |first=Jack |date=December 19, 1969 |title=Senate Votes Study On Fast Rail Link To Dulles Airport |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B5 |id={{ProQuest|143676469}} }} though the [[Dulles International Airport station]] did not open until 2022.{{cite web |last=Hickman |first=Matt |date=November 7, 2022 |title=Washington Metro to debut Dulles Airport–linking Silver Line rail extension |url=https://www.archpaper.com/2022/11/washington-metro-dulles-airport-silver-line-rail-extension/ |access-date=October 19, 2025 |website=The Architect's Newspaper }} A 1996 expansion to the original terminal contained provisions for connections to a future Metro station.{{cite magazine |last1=Wormser |first1=Lisa |last2=Schamess |first2=Gil |date=Jan 1997 |title=Just get me to the plane on time |magazine=Planning |pages=8–11 |volume=63 |issue=1 |id={{ProQuest|206710174}} }} Along the terminal's south or [[airside]] facade, a concourse extends southward. Initially, the southern facade had loading docks for 24 mobile lounges, with 12 on either side of the south concourse. There is a {{Convert|177|ft|4=-tall|adj=mid}}{{Efn|Sometimes cited as {{Convert|193|ft}}{{cite web |last=Verderame |first=Lori |title=Fine Art & Antiques: Art is woven into airport architecture |website=Mainline Media News |date=September 7, 2010 |url=https://www.mainlinemedianews.com/2010/09/07/fine-art-antiques-art-is-woven-into-airport-architecture/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 }}}} [[airport control tower]] above the south concourse.{{harvnb|Architectural Forum|1963|ps=.|page=79 }}{{cite web |last=Rife |first=Bob |date=November 24, 1968 |title=Dulles Airport Ready for Tomorrow's Needs |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-news-leader-dulles-airport-rea/183175950/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Daily News Leader |page=19 }} The tower itself is {{Convert|160|ft}} tall and is topped by a [[radome]] measuring {{Convert|17|ft}} in diameter; the tower was decommissioned in 2007 but remains in place.{{cite news |last=Kelly |first=John |date=March 4, 2023 |title=Radar love: Tracing the changes atop Dulles Airport's iconic tower |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/dc-md-va/2023/03/04/dulles-airport-radome/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 }} The Main Terminal also has four gates known as the Z gates, where aircraft can load and unload passengers directly; these are located along the southern facade, east of the south concourse.{{harvnb|Schwartz|2007|ps=.|page=52 }} South of the terminal is the airport's [[Airport apron|apron]].{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=October 26, 1960 |title=Dallas Terminal Work Racing to Meet Deadline: Airport Plans Call For Construction Through Winter |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=24 |id={{ProQuest|141194180}} }} ==== Facade ==== [[File:Dulles Terminal - 2.jpg|thumb|Exterior view of the northern (landside) colonnade of the terminal (2023)]] The concave roof is supported by two parallel [[colonnade]]s to the north and south, which divide each facade into [[Bay (architecture)|bays]] measuring {{Convert|40|ft}} wide. In the original portion of the terminal, there are 16 columns in each colonnade. The northern colonnade's columns (facing the [[land side]]) are {{Convert|65|ft}} high, while the southern colonnade's columns (facing the [[air side]]) are {{Convert|40|ft}} high.{{Efn|These dimensions are given by several sources. Some sources have given different heights of {{Convert|64|ft}} for the taller columns, or {{convert|45|ft}} for the shorter columns.}} The columns are all made of [[reinforced concrete]], which is [[bush hammer]]ed; the [[rebar]], or reinforcing steel, in the columns was manufactured by [[Bethlehem Steel]].{{cite web |date=February 21, 1963 |title=Steelton Plant Supplies Airport |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-evening-news-steelton-plant-supplies/183169055/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Evening News |page=5 |via=newspapers.com }} Each of the taller columns has {{Convert|20|ST|LT t}} of reinforcing steel, while each of the shorter columns is reinforced by {{Convert|16|ST|LT t}} of steel.{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|page=223|ps=. }} The columns slant outward at an angle of either 10 or 15 degrees,{{cite news |last=Forgey |first=Benjamin |date=September 9, 1995 |title=The Soaring Spirit of Dulles |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1995/09/09/the-soaring-spirit-of-dulles/4cf5db7d-ff54-461c-b0bc-7fbb64731797/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=D01 |id={{ProQuest|307865682}} }} counteracting the forces of suspension cables that carry the roof. At the top of each column are edge beams, which hold the roof's cables in place.{{harvnb|Architectural Record|1960|ps=.|page=178 }}{{Cite magazine |last=Ichniowski |first=Tom |date=April 15, 1996 |title=D.C. Airports' $2.1-Billion Ticket to Fly in Style |magazine=Engineering News-Record |page=26 |volume=236 |issue=15 |id={{ProQuest|235754583}} }} When the terminal was extended west and east in the 1990s, the new columns were built to the same dimensions as the original terminals' columns. The landside columns support a canopy that protrudes {{Convert|43|ft}} above the landside drop-off ramp. The [[Curtain wall (architecture)|curtain walls]] between the columns are made of glass, slanting outward at the same angle as the columns.{{cite web |last=Wells |first=Hugh |date=July 16, 1962 |title=Dulles Builders in Dither |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-dulles-builders-in-ditherh/182940470/ |access-date=October 14, 2025 |website=Evening Star |page=19 }} Each glass pane is placed on rubber [[gasket]]s and fastened to the columns using rubber strips;{{cite news |last=Grant |first=Gerald |date=August 30, 1962 |title=Dulles to Open Nov. 17 With 60 Flights Although Airport Won't Be Completed |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=D1 |id={{ProQuest|141645726}} }} these gaskets tended to fall off after they were installed.{{harvnb|Freeman|1997|page=66|ps=. }} The [[Pittsburgh Plate Glass|Pittsburgh Plate Glass Company]] made {{Convert|70,000|ft2}} of glass for the terminal, which were cut into 1,137 shapes.{{cite web |date=January 24, 1963 |title=Local PPG Plant Provides Glass for Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-jefferson-county-press-times-local-p/183127711/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The Jefferson County Press-Times |page=1 }} The window panes are embedded within aluminum frames, which are curved and tilt outward at their tops.{{harvnb|Architectural Forum|1963|ps=.|page=77 }} The curtain walls in the annexes are similar in style to the original curtain walls, though they use modern gaskets that were less susceptible to falling. ==== Roof ==== The roof is composed of [[precast concrete]] panels, suspended between cables that span the width of the building.{{cite web |last=Giles |first=John Warren |date=October 2, 1960 |title=Dulles Airport—Jet Age Showpiece |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-baltimore-sun-dulles-airportjet-age/182912447/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Baltimore Sun |page=27 |id={{ProQuest|533749900}} }}{{cite web |date=August 9, 1961 |title=Nitterhouse Co. Makes Roof Panels for Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/public-opinion-nitterhouse-co-makes-roo/182930145/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Public Opinion |page=3 }} Nitterhouse Concrete Products in Pennsylvania manufactured the slabs. There are 1,792 concrete slabs in the roof, which each weigh {{convert|800|lb}} and measure {{convert|7.5|in}} thick, including a {{convert|1.5|in||-thick|adj=mid}} styrofoam layer on the underside of each panel. The slabs, which measure {{Convert|8+2/3|by|5+11/12|ft}} across, create a deck spanning {{Convert|89800|ft2}}. The cables, similar in design to the suspenders used on [[suspension bridge]]s, are {{Convert|1|in}} in diameter and are spaced {{Convert|10|ft}} apart. Concrete stiffening ribs encase each of the cables,{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|pages=222–223|ps=. }} preventing the cables from bouncing around; these ribs are {{Convert|14|to|16|in}} deep. Because the columns are slanted outward, the ribs are about {{Convert|160|ft}} or {{Convert|170|ft}} wide.{{harvnb|Architectural Forum|1963|ps=.|page=80 }} To improve acoustics, the roof dips at the centerline of the terminal, reaching as low as {{Convert|26|ft}} or {{Convert|28|ft}}.{{cite web |last=Friedlander |first=Paul J.C. |date=November 11, 1962 |title=Model for Future Airports; a New International Airport for Washington an Airport of Future 'Hungry Locust' The Skeptics Boon to Travel 14 Airlines |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/11/11/archives/model-for-future-airports-a-new-international-airport-for.html |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The roof's centerline slopes down from both ends toward a drainpipe at the center of the building.{{Cite news |last=Sehlstedt |first=Albert Jr. |date=May 3, 1962 |title='Shangri-La' Chantilly Field Passes Passenger Trial Run |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=56, 43 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|534226590}} }} The drainpipe is about {{Convert|30|in}} wide and can drain {{Convert|12500|gal|m3}} from the roof every minute. Water from the drainpipe is funneled into a [[catch basin]] nearby.{{cite web |date=January 14, 1965 |title=Conservation Beautifies Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-news-leader-conservation-beaut/183167387/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Daily News Leader |page=6 }} The roofs over the 1990s extensions are similar in design to the original roof. === Interior === Originally, the terminal spanned {{Convert|500000|ft2}}.{{cite magazine |date=November 11, 1997 |title=Dulles International: From Cornfields to Amber Waves of Planes |magazine=World Airport Week |page=1 |volume=4 |issue=45 |id={{ProQuest|195227374}} }}{{Efn|One source says that the main terminal originally spanned {{Convert|362442|ft2}}.}} During a 1996 expansion, the size of the Main Terminal was more than doubled,{{cite web |date=September 6, 1996 |title=Expanded Dulles terminal dedicated |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/potomac-news-expanded-dulles-terminal-de/183331562/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=Potomac News |page=7 }} increasing to about {{Convert|1.1|e6ft2}}. The interiors were initially designed in a palette of green, blue, brown, and gray hues, to match the landscape.{{cite news |last=Gustaitis |first=Rasa |date=November 19, 1962 |title=Halaby Sees Air Terminal As Garden, U.S. Showcase: Halaby Foresees 'Pressure' Garden to Be Showcase Weather Deters Visitors |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B2 |id={{ProQuest|141591379}} }} Originally, the Main Terminal's upper level was for departing passengers, while the lower level was for arriving passengers. The west and east wings have a combined {{Convert|600000|ft2}} and contain an additional basement level that is not present under the original terminal. ==== Structural and mechanical features ==== The cable roof allowed Saarinen to construct the upper story without columns. The lower story sits on a concrete floor slab, and the upper story's floor slab is made of reinforced concrete. On the lower story, columns are placed at regular intervals, supporting concrete beams above; these beams are aligned with the colonnades on the facade. The lower-story columns flare outward at their bases purely for decorative purposes. The original interiors are divided into [[Bay (architecture)|bays]] measuring {{Convert|40|by|150|ft}}, spanning the terminal's entire width and corresponding to the facade's bays. Each interior bay could be configured with its own ticket counter, baggage facility, concessions, and two loading bays for mobile lounges. Saarinen's original design allowed {{convert|40|ft}} bays to be added on either end of the terminal as necessary.{{harvnb|Architectural Record|1960|ps=.|page=181 }} Saarinen's master plan for Dulles Airport called for service buildings both east and west of the Main Terminal; these structures were designed with low roofs so they did not obstruct views from the Main Terminal. The original service building, to the east, included equipment for hot and chilled water production.{{Cite magazine |last=Marstiller |first=Ted |date=Feb 1999 |title=Engineered for energy savings |magazine=Consulting-Specifying Engineer |pages=32–38 |volume=25 |issue=2 |id={{ProQuest|220602213}} }} When the terminal was completed, it was cooled by two large refrigeration units, which had a daily cooling capacity equivalent to {{Convert|2|e6lb|-2}} of ice.{{cite news |date=April 16, 1960 |title=Huge Air Conditioners To Cool Dulles Airport: New Bed Space |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B11 |id={{ProQuest|141076863}} }} ==== Facilities ==== [[File:2022-03-24_13_43_30_UTC_minus_4_Ticketing_and_check-in_section_within_the_main_terminal_at_Washington_Dulles_International_Airport_in_the_Dulles_section_of_Sterling,_Loudoun_County,_Virginia.jpg|thumb|Interior of the upper level, with ticket counters at left and the curtain wall at right (2022)]] When the terminal was built, there were ticket counters on the upper level, and conveyor belts that brought baggage to a loading area in the basement. The ticket counters were originally grouped into three clusters. In addition, there were various stores, three seating areas with aluminum and vinyl benches, along with two large departure screens.{{cite news |last=Bradley |first=Wendell P. |date=November 14, 1962 |title=Dulles Incomplete, But Ready to Open: Typical Trip |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|141526323}} }} The original design included very few stores,{{cite news |last=Barbaro |first=Michael |date=July 4, 2005 |title=A Traveler's Ritual: Eat, Shop and Leave |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/2005/07/04/a-travelers-ritual-eat-shop-and-leave/21d2ae75-1ce0-4d1b-8732-99a34006b12e/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 }} since it was not originally envisioned as a place to spend extended amounts of time.{{cite web |last=Barbaro |first=Michael |date=July 17, 2005 |title=Traveler's ritual: eat, shop and leave |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-santa-fe-new-mexican-travelers-ritu/183358767/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=The Santa Fe New Mexican |page=F003 }} When the terminal opened, there were 24 mobile-lounge gates. Many of the mobile-lounge gates were subsequently closed with the implementation of stringent security procedures, and some of these gates were infilled with glass in the 1990s. When the terminal was expanded west and east in the 1990s, stores and ticket counters were built in both wings; the annexes have similar terrazzo floors and concrete surfaces to the original terminal. Until the 2000s, the upper story also had security-screening areas.{{cite web |date=October 15, 2007 |title=$1.3 billion Dulles renovation advances |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/usa-today-13-billion-dulles-renovation/183359107/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=USA Today |page=21 }} The lower, or ground, story initially contained regional and commuter airline gates, along with offices and baggage carousels. The lower level also includes a "Dulles Diamond" security screening facility for frequent travelers,{{cite news |last=Yu |first=Roger |date=September 14, 2009 |title=Airport check-in |work=USA Today |page=B.6 |id={{ProQuest|409113185}} }}{{cite news |date=September 13, 2009 |title=comingandgoing |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/travel/2009/09/13/comingandgoing/f1828b59-4efa-49dd-8958-f18ceb077ea2/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=F.3 |id={{ProQuest|410322043}} }} as well as baggage carousels and a baggage-sorting facility in the west wing. Escalators connect the upper and lower levels, allowing arriving passengers to pick up their baggage. The south concourse had marble tables and upholstered seats. There was also a reflecting pool in the south concourse, along with lounges on a balcony level overlooking the concourse. Basements under both wings accommodate baggage handling facilities, and there are two basements beneath the original terminal.{{cite news |last=Weiss |first=Eric M. |date=August 19, 2008 |title=Dulles Updates Its People Movers |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2008/08/19/dulles-updates-its-people-movers/38f86416-a9c0-46f8-91ef-bd3204529544/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B.1 |id={{ProQuest|410248159}} }} The original structure's first or upper basement contains security checkpoints spanning {{convert|121700|sqft|m2}};{{Cite magazine |date=September 28, 2009 |title=Security Shortlines |magazine=Air Safety Week |volume=23 |issue=35 |id={{ProQuest|204710882}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=September 14, 2009 |title=New Passenger Security Screening Areas Open at Dulles International Airport Tomorrow |url=http://www.mwaa.com/file/pr2009_09_14.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101216123050/http://mwaa.com/file/pr2009_09_14.pdf |archive-date=December 16, 2010 |access-date=October 12, 2010 |publisher=Metropolitan Washington Airport Authority Office of Public Affairs }} the {{Convert|8500|ft2|adj=on}} Capital One Lounge is located between the western and eastern checkpoints.{{cite web |last=Clabaugh |first=Jeff |date=September 7, 2023 |title=Capital One opens Dulles Airport lounge |url=https://wtop.com/business-finance/2023/09/capital-one-opens-dulles-airport-lounge/ |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=WTOP News }} The second or lower basement contains a {{convert|54500|ft2|adj=on}} station for the [[AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)|AeroTrain]] people-mover system. The taxi and bus–limousine drop-off areas lead directly to the terminal's upper level, and a ramp and escalators lead from the private automobile drop-off areas to the upper level. A {{Convert|1000|ft|4=-long|adj=mid}} underpass with [[moving walkway]]s links the Main Terminal to parking garages and the Dulles International Airport station. The underpass is accessed from the terminal via elevators{{cite web |last=Cline |first=Nathaniel |date=October 12, 2022 |title=Dulles to join Reagan as the most public transit-accessible Virginia airports |url=https://virginiamercury.com/2022/10/12/dulles-to-join-reagan-as-the-most-public-transit-accessible-virginia-airports/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Virginia Mercury }} and a pair of escalators.{{cite web |last=Iannelli |first=Nick |date=November 22, 2022 |title=Here's what you'll experience walking from Metro's new Dulles station to the airport |url=https://wtop.com/tracking-metro-24-7/2022/11/heres-what-youll-experience-walking-from-metros-new-dulles-station-to-the-airport/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=WTOP News }} Another {{Convert|1000|ft|4=-long|adj=mid}} tunnel leads south from the Main Terminal to midfield concourse B. Escalators and elevators also descend to the basements.{{Cite magazine |last=Ventimiglia |first=Diana |date=Jun 2012 |title=Forward Progress |magazine=Lighting Design + Application |pages=38–41 |volume=42 |issue=6 |id={{ProQuest|1025740021}} }} === Airside transport === {{Further|Mobile lounge|AeroTrain (Dulles International Airport)}} [[File:Dulles International Airport mobile lounges 00769v (1).jpg|thumb|The terminal with its original mobile lounges ({{circa|1962}})]] Initially, after passengers were processed at the Main Terminal, they were transported directly to planes via mobile lounges.{{harvnb|Pelkonen|Albrecht|2006|page=304|ps=. }}{{harvnb|Schwartz|2007|ps=.|page=50 }} The original mobile lounges were manufactured by [[Budd Company]] and [[Chrysler]].{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=November 26, 1961 |title=FAA Approves Mobile Lounges For Dulles Plane Passengers |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|141387203}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=November 29, 1961 |title=Airport in Washington To Get Mobile Lounges |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/11/29/archives/airport-in-washington-to-get-mobile-lounges.html |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} They were similar to [[Airport bus#Airside transfer|airside transfer buses]], except that the lounges were intended as movable extensions of the terminal itself,{{harvnb|Architectural Record|1960|ps=.|page=180 }} with floors at the same height as the departure level. Each lounge had doorways and adjustable ramps at both ends, along with seats similar to those in the Main Terminal. Though the floor could be raised and lowered to accommodate different plane models' heights, it could not rise above {{Convert|13|ft}}.{{cite web |date=November 6, 1969 |title=New Wheeled Airport Lounge Shown |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1969/11/06/archives/new-wheeled-airport-lounge-shown.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} Each mobile lounge could travel at a top speed of about {{cvt|25|mph}}.{{Cite news |last=Riley |first=Arthur |date=February 22, 1963 |title=No More of Those Long Terminal Hikes: Chrysler Lounge Carries You to Waiting Jet |work=Boston Globe |page=35 |issn=0743-1791 |id={{ProQuest|275849812}} }} Departure times originally reflected when the lounges left the terminal, and larger planes were served by multiple lounges. The Plane Mate, a variant of the mobile lounge, was introduced in the early 1970s{{cite web |last=Roth |first=Maggie |date=September 23, 2025 |title=Dulles' People Movers Could Remain Essential for 20 Years |url=https://northernvirginiamag.com/things-to-do/travel/2025/09/23/dulles-people-movers-could-remain-essential-for-20-years/ |access-date=October 11, 2025 |website=Northern Virginia Magazine }} to accommodate [[wide-body aircraft]].{{Cite news |last=Pillsbury |first=Fred |date=November 28, 1978 |title=Airports: Living with the noise |work=Boston Globe |page=36 |issn=0743-1791 |id={{ProQuest|747068778}} }} In contrast to the lower capacity of the original lounges,{{Efn|Sources disagree on whether the original lounges could fit 90 or 100 passengers.}} the Plane Mates could fit 150 passengers and could rise higher than the original lounges.{{cite news |last=Mathews |first=Jay |date=August 19, 1973 |title=Fire Hazard Of Mobile Lounge Cited |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|148406052}} }} Saarinen considered the mobile lounges a solution to three problems—they shortened the walking distance to the plane, reduced [[taxiing]] distances, and allowed greater [[Airport apron|apron]] flexibility.{{Cite news |last=Sehlstedt |first=Albert Jr. |date=November 19, 1962 |title=Airways and Spaceways |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=30 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|540217418}} }}{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|page=216|ps=. }}{{harvnb|Román|2003|page=116|ps=. }} When the terminal was developed in the 1960s, jet planes could not fit web |date=September 28, 1962 |title=Target Date Set for Dulles Field; F.A.A. Hopes Capital Airport Will Be Ready Nov. 19 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/09/28/archives/target-date-set-for-dulles-field-faa-hopes-capital-airport-will-be.html |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} and allowed Dulles Airport to be built with a single terminal, smaller in size than other airports' terminals. They were also intended to increase operational flexibility, because planes no longer had to unload passengers next to the terminal,{{cite web |last=Stepp |first=John W. |date=April 8, 1959 |title=Mobile Lounges to Haul Passengers to Jet Planes at Chantilly Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-mobile-lounges-to-haul-pass/182907161/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Evening Star |page=13 }} while also reducing airlines' taxiing fees and keeping aircraft emissions away from the terminal.{{Cite news |last=Bennett |first=Stephen A. |date=January 20, 1964 |title=Airways And Spaceways: Mobile Lounges At Dulles Prove Worth In Big Snow |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=20 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|540113127}} }} Passengers also did not have to walk more than a few hundred feet.{{Efn|Sources disagree on whether the lounges reduced airline passengers' average walking distance to either {{Convert|150|ft}}, {{Convert|200|ft}}, or {{Convert|300|ft}}. One newspaper said that passengers needed to walk just 22 steps from the main entrance to the ticket counter and another 48 steps to the lounges.}} Retrospectively, observers noted that the lounges |postscript=none}}; {{cite news |last=Henderson |first=Nell |date=March 24, 1989 |title=Mobile Lounges At Dulles To Be Tested |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1989/03/24/mobile-lounges-at-dulles-to-be-tested/21434b15-960b-4513-ba39-4391c1c58296/ |access-date=October 19, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B01 |id={{ProQuest|307144144}} }} and that passengers making [[connecting flight]]s had to wait for multiple lounges.{{cite book |last=Gottdiener |first=Mark |url=https://archive.org/details/lifeinairsurvivi0000gott |url-access=registration |title=Life in the Air: Surviving the New Culture of Air Travel |date=2001 |publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing PLC |isbn=978-0-7425-0029-7 |pages=63–64 |access-date=October 18, 2025 }} When the midfield concourses were built in the 1980s, the mobile lounges began traveling to these concourses instead.{{cite web |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/usa-today-dulles-hopes-to-regain-its-cut/182863910/ |access-date=October 12, 2025 |website=USA Today |page=21 }} The [[AeroTrain (Dulles International Distinctive Mobile Lounge System with AeroTrain |url=https://www.thetransportpolitic.com/2010/01/26/dulles-airport-replaces-distinctive-mobile-lounge-system-with-aerotrain/ |access-date=October 11, 2025 |website=The Transport Politic }} {{As of|2025}}, Dulles Airport's operator [[Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority]] retains 19 of Saarinen's mobile lounges and 30 Plane Mates, which |url=https://www.ffxnow.com/2025/09/22/dulles-mobile-lounges-could-last-another-two-decades-airport-officials-say/ |access-date=October 19, 2025 |website=FFXnow }} There are also plans to extend the
