|first=Mimi |date=July 23, 2025 |title=Dulles to people movers: TTYL |url=https://www.axios.com/local/washington-dc/2025/07/23/dulles-airport-master-plan-expansion |access-date=October 11, 2025 |website=Axios (website) }} the potential expansion of the AeroTrain would make the remaining mobile lounges obsolete. == History == === Development === The [[81st United States Congress|U.S. Congress]] passed the Washington Inner Airports Act in 1950 to provide funding for a new airport in the [[Washington metropolitan area]].{{harvnb|Mehaffy|2005|ps=.|page=S4 }}{{harvnb|Stroud|1980|ps=.|page=557 }} This directly led to the creation of what became [[Dulles International Airport]] in [[Chantilly, Virginia]]. President [[Dwight Eisenhower]] selected the {{Convert|8000|acre|adj=on}} Chantilly site in January 1958,{{cite news |date=January 15, 1958 |title=Ike Selects Chantilly as Airport Site: Says Area Meets Requirements for Space and Safety By Elsie Carper Staff Reporter Ike Selects Chantilly as Airport Site |work=The Washington Post and Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|148933144}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |last=Beveridge |first=George |date=January 14, 1958 |title=Chantilly Chosen as Airport Site |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-chantilly-chosen-as-airport/182866662/ |access-date=October 12, 2025 |work=Evening Star |pages=1, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-chantilly-airport/182866604/ 6] }} and the U.S. government acquired the land that August.{{Cite magazine |date=August 4, 1958 |title=Taxpayers Build Another Airport: Work on Washington's new airport at Chantilly, Va., began August 1 when the government officially took possession of the 8,000-acre site. As usual, Uncle Sam is footing the bills |magazine=Railway Age |page=24 |volume=145 |issue=5 |id={{ProQuest|882952002}} }} The airport was officially named in 1959 after [[John Foster Dulles]], the [[United States Secretary of State]] under Eisenhower.{{cite news |date=October 1, 1961 |title=It's Officially Dulles Airport, But the FAA Has Other Ideas |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A25 |id={{ProQuest|141437816}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=July 16, 1959 |title=What Goes On Here |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-washington-daily-news-what-goes-on-h/182871315/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Washington Daily News |page=5 }} The airport and its Main Terminal were originally controlled directly by the U.S. federal government through the [[Federal Aviation Administration]] (FAA).{{cite book |title=Federal Aviation Regulations, Change 1, Part 159 - National Capital Airports, May 2, 1996 |date=1993 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YLff3Db7WS4C&dq=DULLES+AIRPORT+OPERATED+BY+Federal+Aviation+Administration+1987&pg=PA79 |access-date=October 27, 2025 |page=P-79 }} ==== Design ==== [[File:2022-03-24 13 47 19 UTC minus 4 Ticketing and check-in section within the main terminal at Washington Dulles International Airport in the Dulles section of Sterling, Loudoun County, Virginia.jpg|thumb|Interior (2022)]] The [[Civil Aeronautics Administration (United States)|Civil Aeronautics Administration]] (CAA) selected [[Eero Saarinen]] of [[Bloomfield Hills, Michigan]], in May 1958 to design several of Dulles Airport's buildings, including its Main Terminal and control tower.{{cite news |date=May 1, 1958 |title=Designers Are Selected For Chantilly |work=The Washington Post and Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=C11 |id={{ProQuest|149109271}} }}{{cite web |date=May 1, 1958 |title=Airport Project Given Saarinen |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/jackson-citizen-patriot-airport-project/182872787/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Jackson Citizen Patriot |page=33 }} [[Ammann & Whitney]], who led the airport's overall design, had previously worked with Saarinen on [[Ellinikon International Airport]]'s terminal. At the time, Saarinen was busy designing the [[TWA Flight Center]] at [[Idlewild Airport]] in New York.{{harvnb|Román|2003|page=111|ps=. }} Saarinen and Ammann & Whitney worked in collaboration with the airport's mechanical engineering firm [[Burns & McDonnell]] and the consultant Charles Landrum to collect data for the design of Dulles Airport's Main Terminal. They studied airport operations, including the distances passengers had to walk to access planes, at airports across the U.S.; the team found that, on average, passengers had to walk {{Convert|900|ft}} from terminal to plane.{{cite web |date=September 1, 1960 |title=Oracle |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/transcript-telegram-oracle/182934148/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Transcript-Telegram |page=28 }} The design team was particularly focused on reducing passengers' walking distances, reducing [[taxiing]] costs, and increasing flexibility of the apron.{{harvnb|Architectural Record|1960|ps=.|page=179 }} Furthermore, they anticipated that Dulles Airport would need 60 [[Gate (airport)|gates]] by 1975 to accommodate increasing demand. Saarinen sketched his initial designs on [[legal paper]].{{cite web |last=Edwards |first=Ellen |date=February 26, 1978 |title=Architecture as Art |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-miami-herald-architecture-as-artell/183188673/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Miami Herald |pages=1N, [https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-miami-herald-200-years-of-plans-make/183188651/ 2N] }} One early design proposal, by Boyd Anderson of Ammann & Whitney, called for suspension cables between the ground and roof; after Saarinen expressed his satisfaction, the design team instead proposed a cable roof. The CAA reviewed Saarinen's preliminary ideas for the terminal in October 1958. A key component of the plan was mobile lounges that would travel from the terminal directly to planes, eliminating many of the inflexibilities of jetways and fixed gates.{{cite news |date=October 31, 1958 |title=Airport Starts Runway Work |work=The Washington Post and Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B5 |id={{ProQuest|149072220}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |last=Norling |first=Kristin |date=October 30, 1958 |title=Airport May Give Passengers a Lift |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-washington-daily-news-airport-may-gi/182872976/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Washington Daily News |page=5 }} The terminal itself was tentatively planned to have separate levels for departing and arriving passengers.{{cite web |last=Leslie |first=Frank |date=April 12, 1959 |title=Aviation World |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/tulsa-world-aviation-worldfrank-leslie/182902069/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Tulsa World |page=10 }} Contracts for clearing and grading the site had been awarded by the end of 1958, but no contracts for the terminal had been awarded yet.{{cite news |date=December 20, 1958 |title=Baltimore Firm Submits Low Bid on Airport Job |work=The Washington Post and Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A9 |id={{ProQuest|148961030}} }} The terminal design was still in progress by early 1959, at which point it was planned to span {{Convert|300,000|ft2}}. Although no details had been announced at the time, the [[Evening Star (Washington D.C.)|''Evening Star'']] described the design as "something revolutionary". Saarinen's friend [[Charles Eames]] prepared a short film about the mobile lounges to convince airport officials of their efficacy.{{harvnb|McQuade|1962|page=104|ps=. }} The FAA (then known as the [[Federal Aviation Agency]]) announced details of Saarinen's design in January 1960.{{cite web |date=January 31, 1960 |title=Design is Shown for Dulles Field; New Capital Airport to Use 'Mobile Lounges' to Cut Walking Distances |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1960/01/31/archives/design-is-shown-for-dulles-field-new-capital-airport-to-use-mobile.html |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The plans called for a {{convert|600|by|150|ft|adj=on|m|}} double-level structure, with concrete piers supporting a concave curved roof; the building could be doubled in size. To reduce confusion, departing and arriving passengers were segregated on different levels. Saarinen and his associates wanted the design to symbolize the [[Jet Age]] while also complementing the classical [[architecture of Washington, D.C.]]{{harvnb|Merkel|2005|page=217|ps=. }} The [[control tower]] and mobile lounges were designed in conjunction with the terminal; the lounges in particular made it possible to reduce the building's size, since long passageways were no longer needed. The final design, including mobile lounges, was selected after the FAA examined over 100 proposals. ==== Construction ==== The FAA awarded contracts for the terminal's heating and cooling systems in August 1959.{{cite news |date=August 28, 1959 |title=Three Contracts Let for Airport |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=D2 |id={{ProQuest|140913405}} }} That October, it ordered a prototype of a mobile lounge{{cite news |date=October 14, 1959 |title=Contract Let For Chantilly's Mobile Lounges |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B4 |id={{ProQuest|140971628}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=October 14, 1959 |title=Jetport Lounge on Wheels |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/detroit-free-press-jetport-lounge-on-whe/182908248/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Detroit Free Press |page=40 |agency=United Press International }} and awarded a contract for the terminal's telephone service.{{cite news |date=October 23, 1959 |title=Independent Phone Firm Gets Set at New Airport |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B3 |id={{ProQuest|141005139}} }} The FAA also built [[settling basin]]s for temporary use until a permanent sewage system for the terminal could be built.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=May 18, 1960 |title=3 Airport Sewage Ponds Will Safeguard Potomac: On-Site Plant To Be Standby For Interceptor Construction Underway Supremely Confident Endorsed by WSSC |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141137902}} }} The FAA began soliciting bids for the terminal building itself in January 1960{{cite web |date=January 14, 1960 |title=Bids Are Sought for Terminal at Dulles Field |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/danville-register-and-bee-bids-are-sough/182926225/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Danville Register and Bee |page=22 |agency=Associated Press }} and reviewed the bids the next month.{{cite news |date=February 29, 1960 |title=FAA to See Bids On Airport Job |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B6 |id={{ProQuest|141132855}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=February 29, 1960 |title=What Goes On Here |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-washington-daily-news-what-goes-on-h/182926320/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Washington Daily News |page=5 }} The Corbetta Construction Company of New York City submitted the lowest bid, for $4,432,000,{{cite news |date=March 9, 1960 |title=N.Y. Firm's Bid Low on Airport Job |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B9 |id={{ProQuest|141149307}} }}{{cite web |date=March 2, 1960 |title=$4.4 Million Bid Offered on Part of Airport Work |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-44-million-bid-offered-on/182922476/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Evening Star |page=2 }} and was subsequently awarded the construction contract.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=December 13, 1960 |title=Six-Month Delay Seen In New Airport Opening |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B6 |id={{ProQuest|141157362}} }} That April, workers began grading the terminal's site and laying [[Foundation (engineering)|foundations]].{{cite web |date=April 20, 1960 |title=Dulles Airport Slated to Open Next Summer |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-free-lance-star-dulles-airport-slate/182917529/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Free Lance-Star |page=19 }} Models of the Main Terminal were displayed at [[Washington National Airport]] in August 1960.{{cite news |last=Kornberg |first=Warren |date=August 20, 1960 |title=Airlines Oversubscribe Dulles Space Even Before New Airport Is Finished |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=D2 |id={{ProQuest|141084285}} }} By then, the U.S. federal government (which originally operated the airport) had [[Overselling|oversubscribed]] all of the ticket counter space and the gates.{{cite web |date=August 20, 1960 |title=Capital's Jetport Shown in Models; Terminal and Lounges for Duties Field Displayed by Aviation Agency |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1960/08/20/archives/capitals-jetport-shown-in-models-terminal-and-lounges-for-duties.html |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The demand for ticket counter space was already one-third higher than what was available.[[File:Dulles International Airport (1970).jpg|thumb|The original terminal seen from the northeast (1970)]]The Main Terminal's structural work was half complete by October 1960. At that point, concrete for the lower level had been poured, and workers had erected steel framework on the north and south side of the building, in preparation for the construction of the columns. By the end of the year, the airport was unlikely to be completed by its originally-projected opening date of July 1961,{{cite web |date=December 13, 1960 |title=Dulles Airport Terminal Lagging, Quesada Says |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/evening-star-dulles-airport-terminal-lag/182926445/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Evening Star |page=16 }} so outgoing FAA administrator [[Pete Quesada]] postponed the opening date by one year.{{cite news |date=January 5, 1961 |title=Dulles Airport Opening Now Fixed at July, 1962 |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A6 |id={{ProQuest|141383095}} }} By June 1961, the airport's original $85{{nbsp}}million budget had more than doubled to $175{{nbsp}}million, and FAA administrator [[Najeeb Halaby]] said the new terminal would be overcrowded by 1967.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=June 1, 1961 |title=Dulles Airport to Cost $175 Million, Not 85: Dulles Cost Jumps to $175 Million |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|141485309}} }} Due to a lack of federal funding, the building's initial length was truncated from {{Convert|1200|to|600|ft}}. The terminal was still under construction when Saarinen suddenly died in September 1961,{{cite web |date=September 2, 1961 |title=Private Funeral Held for Eero Saarinen |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-flint-journal-private-funeral-held-f/182935812/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The Flint Journal |page=11 }} at which point it was budgeted at $12{{nbsp}}million. For the construction of each column, workers poured concrete around multiple tons of steel [[rebar]].{{cite magazine |date=Sep 1961 |title=Saarinen |url=https://www.usmodernist.org/AF/AF-1961-09.pdf |magazine=Architectural Forum |page=113 |volume=115 |issue=3 }} The rebar in each column surrounded a metal cage, from which a worker oversaw the pour until it was nearly complete; the cage was then encased in concrete. Workers pre-stressed the roof's cables by loading sandbags onto them, thus allowing the cables to carry the roof panels without sagging significantly. The cables were strung between each pair of columns, then bent into shape using concrete blocks and encased in concrete; their installation required many complex computations. The concrete roof ribs were test-loaded after being poured. No stationary [[scaffolding]] was used for the terminal's construction, though the roof was built using a movable scaffold. ==== Completion ==== Thirteen airlines had leased space at the airport by late 1961.{{cite news |date=December 3, 1961 |title=Big Lounges On Wheels Stir Airlines: $4.6 Million Cost Too High, FAA Warned |work=New York Herald Tribune |page=9 |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|1325764732}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=December 2, 1961 |title=Transport News and Notes; Lines Score F.A.A.'s Paying $4,600,000 for 'Mobile Lounges' at Dulles Airport |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1961/12/02/archives/transport-news-and-notes-lines-score-faas-paying-4600000-for-mobile.html |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} That November, the FAA awarded a concession for the terminal's bars and restaurants.{{cite web |date=November 11, 1961 |title=Dulles Airport Concession Given |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-dulles-airport-c/182935679/ |access-date=October 13, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=27 }} The FAA paid $4.6{{nbsp}}million for the terminal's first 20 mobile lounges that month, but the airlines hesitated at paying the cost. The airlines were also reluctant to give the FAA specifications for space at the terminal until they knew how much their leases would cost. As such, that December, Halaby threatened to take over the design of each airline's spaces unless the airlines provided specifications within two weeks.{{cite news |date=December 22, 1961 |title=Airlines Given 2 Weeks to Decide On Space Required at Dulles Airport |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141412064}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite news |last=Loory |first=Stuart H. |date=December 21, 1961 |title=Quit Fighting, FAA's Halaby Tells Airlines |work=New York Herald Tribune |page=21 |issn=1941-0646 |id={{ProQuest|1326275379}} }} By then, the control tower was 60% complete.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=December 28, 1961 |title=Dulles Terminal Design Applauded by Art Panel: Panel Members Wanted Ideas |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141254928}} }} The airlines agreed to lease the Main Terminal's {{convert|456|ft|adj=on}} ticket counter in January 1962, having petitioned for a longer counter.{{cite news |last=Hailey |first=Albon B. |date=January 11, 1962 |title=Airlines Agree to Use Dulles After Reaching Accord With FAA on Space Allocations: Talks Set Feb.1 On Rental Costs And Landing Fees Space For 14 Lines Counter Space Fixed |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=D1 |id={{ProQuest|141783171}} |postscript=none}}; {{Cite news |last=Sehlstedt |first=Albert Jr. |date=January 11, 1962 |title=Interest in New Airport Hinted: Airline Representative Comments on Use of Dulles |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=46 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|542448452}} }} Disputes over fees continued until that June, when the FAA and the airlines agreed on a schedule of operating fees for the mobile lounges and the terminal's space.{{cite web |date=May 4, 1962 |title=Dulles Field Fees Settled by F.A.A.; Agreement on User Charges Reached With 13 Airlines |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/05/04/archives/dulles-field-fees-settled-by-faa-agreement-on-user-charges-reached.html |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |last=Shafer |first=Clyde |date=May 6, 1962 |title=Aviation |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-tampa-tribune-aviationclyde-shafer/183112553/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The Tampa Tribune |page=72 }} The terminal's contractors began working double shifts in April 1962 after Halaby threatened to penalize contractors for not completing the terminal by October 1.{{cite web |date=April 27, 1962 |title=Double Work Shift at Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-daily-advance-double-work-shift-at-d/183113194/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The Daily Advance |agency=Associated Press }} During mid-1962, the FAA solicited bids for the construction of service spaces for the airlines.{{cite news |date=June 11, 1962 |title=Dulles Asks Business Space Bids: Estimates Sought On Service Areas For 14 Airlines |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141610386}} }} Builders had difficulties constructing the windows; as late as June 1962, none of the glass had been installed.{{cite web |last=Whitley |first=Tyler |date=June 7, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport Construction Drags |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-richmond-news-leader-dulles-airport/182941378/ |access-date=October 14, 2025 |website=The Richmond News Leader |page=20 }} Workers eventually built a custom protractor to cut the glass. Because the windows were to slope outward, workers fitted gaskets around each window to prevent them from tipping over. The FAA announced in August 1962 that the terminal and the rest of the airport would be dedicated that November.{{Cite news |date=August 25, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport Dedication Set |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=17 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|542387593}} }} By then, workers were finishing the interior, while airport staff were practicing with the mobile lounges. Numerous shops had been leased out, and additional retailers leased space at the terminal that October.{{cite news |date=October 4, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport Leases Signed for 7 Concessions |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=C26 |id={{ProQuest|141735756}} }} As late as a few days before the opening, many parts of the terminal were still incomplete.{{cite web |date=November 15, 1962 |title=Dulles Airport to Be Dedicated; Bust of Former Cabinet Aide to Be Presented Saturday |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/11/15/archives/dulles-airport-to-be-dedicated-bust-of-former-cabinet-aide-to-be.html |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The final cost was estimated at approximately $16{{nbsp}}million. === Opening and early use === [[File:Dulles Airport terminal windows.jpg|thumb|The western end of the terminal, facing the landside facade (2025)]] On November 17, 1962, former president Eisenhower and U.S. President [[John F. Kennedy]] dedicated the airport with a ceremony at the terminal, attended by an estimated 60,000 people.{{cite news |last=Munsey |first=Everard |date=November 18, 1962 |title=Airport Finishing Work Interrupted for Opening: Service Stars Monday |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141672841}} }} The first passengers began using the terminal two days later,{{cite news |date=November 20, 1962 |title=First Flights Land At Dulles Airfield: Passengers Praise Operation Traffic Is Light Concessionaires Moving In |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141602823}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=November 20, 1962 |title=Service Initiated at Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-press-service-initiated-at-dulles/183127019/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=Daily Press |page=12 }} and the terminal recorded 25,000 tourists on its first full Sunday of operation.{{cite news |last=Hymes |first=Donald L. |date=November 26, 1962 |title=25,000 Visit New Dulles Airport; Going 'Surprisingly Well,' Says FAA |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|141685041}} }} Some final work was still ongoing, with 15% of the work still incomplete at the time of opening.{{cite web |last=Howard |first=Tom |date=November 10, 1963 |title=Dulles Airport: Its Debits and Credits |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-dulles-airport/183132150/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=36 }} The terminal quickly became a symbol of the new airport,{{cite news |last=Baker |first=Leonard |date=November 16, 1962 |title=Airport for the Future: Dulles International Airport, Which Will Be Dedicated Tomorrow, is Designed for the Aviation of the 70s. But Critics Say the Field Near Washington is a Losing Gamble |work=Newsday |page=1C |issn=2574-5298 |id={{ProQuest|899189314}} }} and it received positive acclaim, in part because its mobile lounges made the planes entirely [[Accessibility|accessible]].{{cite web |last=Haugland |first=Vern |date=December 18, 1962 |title=Public Pleased With Dulles International Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/danville-register-and-bee-public-pleased/183126066/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=Danville Register and Bee |page=5 |agency=Associated Press }} Travelers often threw coins into the terminal's reflecting pool; the proceeds were donated to charity.{{cite magazine |date=May 10, 1965 |title=Where's Everybody? |magazine=Newsweek |page=89 |volume=65 |issue=19 |id={{ProQuest|1850828062}} }} The FAA leased out a [[duty-free shop]] at the terminal in early 1963,{{Cite news |date=March 14, 1963 |title=No-duty Store Set for Dulles: Cigarette, Liquor Bargains Planned for D. C. Airport |work=The Baltimore Sun |page=10 |issn=1930-8965 |id={{ProQuest|535589136}} }} and a restaurant opened there that November, at which point the terminal was basically complete. Dulles was initially considered a [[white elephant]], being far from Washington, D.C., with few flights;{{cite news |last=Davis |first=J.W. |date=April 17, 1966 |title=Dulles Airport: Its future keeps being postponed |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=NKZQAAAAIBAJ&pg=6701%2C3637610 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211122093728/https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=NKZQAAAAIBAJ&pg=6701%2C3637610 |archive-date=November 22, 2021 |access-date=November 10, 2020 |newspaper=The Register-Guard |page=10A }} this had a negative effect on the terminal concessionaires' business.{{cite web |date=November 20, 1964 |title=Business Lagging at Dulles Airport; But F.A.A. Is Confident New Terminal Will Prosper |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/20/archives/business-lagging-at-dulles-airport-but-faa-is-confident-new.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} ''[[Newsweek]]'' said that staff sometimes outnumbered passengers, and ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote that "the terminal has entertained nearly twice as many viewers as travelers".{{cite web |last=Loftus |first=Joseph A. |date=November 17, 1963 |title=At Dulles Airport; Traffic Is Light Year After Opening-- Buses Into Washington a Problem The Grumbling Across the Potomac Choice of Routes Easy Does It Big Year |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1963/11/17/archives/at-dulles-airport-traffic-is-light-year-after-opening-buses-into.html |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} Another source said that "once a visitor could roll a bowling ball from one end ... without hitting anyone".{{cite web |last=McCaffrey |first=Scott |date=June 4, 1995 |title=Dulles renovations modernize facility that was neglected |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/sun-news-dulles-renovations-modernize-fa/183325085/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=Sun-News |page=51 }} Conversely, the terminal was popular as a tourist attraction,''{{cite web |last=McDowell |first=Charles Jr. |date=August 15, 1963 |title=The New Dulles Airport: Dream in the Boondocks |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/bristol-herald-courier-the-new-dulles-ai/183168856/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Bristol Herald Courier |page=4 }}'' and the mobile lounges had become more popular than expected;{{cite news |date=November 17, 1963 |title=New Dulles Airport Far from Success |work=Chicago Tribune |page=27 |issn=1085-6706 |id={{ProQuest|179314414}} }} many visitors paid just to ride the lounges.{{cite web |date=April 1, 1973 |title=Dulles Airport Braces for Expansion |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/04/01/archives/dulles-airport-braces-for-expansion-chaos-is-expected.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The terminal and airport continued to experience lower-than-expected patronage in the mid-1960s. Two of the terminal's concessionaires had gone out of business by 1966, while other concessionaires paid discounted rents. At that point, there were somewhat less than a million annual passengers, and only half the mobile lounges were needed.{{cite news |last=Schorr |first=Burt |date=April 5, 1966 |title='Airport of Tomorrow,' Washington's Dulles, Has Problems Aplenty: Distant Field Operates at Some 20% of Capacity; Jets' Debut At National Is New Threat 'Airport of Tomorrow,' Washington's Dulles, Has Problems Aplenty |work=The Wall Street Journal |page=1 |issn=0099-9660 |id={{ProQuest|133126159}} }} In 1968, the lower level flooded, causing some damage to the terminal.{{cite news |last=Burchard |first=Hank |date=August 13, 1968 |title=Flood Buckles Dulles Tower Wall |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|143464431}} }} Patronage steadily increased; by 1969, some concessionaires had recorded their first profits.{{cite news |last=Curry |first=William N. |date=June 11, 1970 |title=Stretch Jet Key At Dulles: Dulles Still Dull Most Of the Time |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=G1 |id={{ProQuest|147819162}} }} === 1970s and early 1980s === By the early 1970s, the FAA anticipated that the terminal's usage would increase sixfold, from 2 to 12{{nbsp}}million, within a decade.{{cite news |last=Samuelson |first=Robert J. |date=January 5, 1970 |title=6-Fold Jump Expected In Passengers at Dulles: Opposition Seen |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=37 |id={{ProQuest|147907390}} }}{{cite web |last=Donnelly |first=Jon |date=November 20, 1972 |title=Dulles Airport Is Alive and Relatively Healthy |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-bee-dulles-airport-is-alive-and-rela/183180820/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Bee |page=29 |agency=Associated Press }} To accommodate the increased traffic, the FAA ordered additional mobile lounges and stopped giving tourists rides on the existing lounges, and U.S. President [[Richard Nixon]] allocated $7{{nbsp}}million for a possible expansion of the Main Terminal.{{cite web |last=Ashworth |first=Linda |date=March 22, 1970 |title=Dulles Airport: Future Finally Here, Officials Say |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-dulles-airport/183177628/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=24 }} Early plans called for the building to be lengthened east–west to {{Convert|920|ft}}, increasing hourly capacity from 1,650 to either 2,300 or 2,500 passengers.{{cite web |date=December 12, 1970 |title=$480,000 to Design Dulles Field Job |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/st-louis-post-dispatch-480000-to-desi/183179685/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=St. Louis Post-Dispatch |page=3 |postscript=none}}; {{cite news |last=Curry |first=William N. |date=December 5, 1970 |title=Contract Awarded To Plan Enlarged Terminal at Dulles: National's Load Dips |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B2 |id={{ProQuest|147800493}} }} The architectural firm [[HOK (firm)|Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum]] (HOK) was hired in December 1970 to prepare preliminary designs for the expansion. When the [[National Capital Planning Commission]] (NCPC) approved the plans in 1972,{{cite news |last=Hodge |first=Paul |date=December 8, 1977 |title=Proposal for Expansion at Dulles Criticized as Destructive to Design: Additional Construction Could Mar Appearance Of Dulles Terminal |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=VA_1 |id={{ProQuest|146691670}} }} the project was estimated to cost $12{{nbsp}}million. HOK and [[Peat, Marwick, Mitchell|Peat, Marwick & Mitchell]] were hired to develop an expansion plan for the terminal, but no progress occurred for several years,{{cite web |last=Huxtable |first=Ada Louise |date=December 18, 1977 |title=Architecture View |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1977/12/18/archives/architecture-view-controversy-over-dulles-airport.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }}{{cite web |last=Ashworth |first=Linda |date=March 25, 1976 |title=Study of Dulles Under Way to Update Its Master Plan |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-study-of-dulles/183184620/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=20 |agency=Associated Press }} in part because of funding shortages and insufficient demand.[[File:Dulles Terminal - 3.jpg|thumb|The landside facade (2023)]]The expansion plans were renewed in 1976, when the FAA directed Peat, Marwick & Mitchell to revise the airport's master plan. At that point, the terminal expansion was planned to cost $15{{nbsp}}million; it was to be part of a $150–190{{nbsp}}million overhaul of the airport.{{cite news |last=Morris |first=Wilson |date=March 7, 1977 |title=Full Impact Of Va. Facility Expected to Be Felt in 1990s: DULLES Airport 'of the Future' Full Impact of Dulles Airport Now Expected in 1990s |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C1 |id={{ProQuest|146811920}} }} The NCPC expressed concerns that the east–west annexes would overshadow the original design, and preservationists advocated for the terminal to be designated as a landmark, restricting changes to the structure. Ultimately, HOK designed two small annexes along the southern facade for additional mobile lounge gates. These annexes measured {{Convert|50|ft}} wide, about the same as the mobile lounges' lengths, and were built in a similar style to the original terminal.{{cite magazine |last=Perkins |first=Bradford |date=Jul 1981 |title=Preserving the landmarks of the Modern Movement |url=https://www.usmodernist.org/AR/AR-1981-07.pdf |magazine=Architectural Record |pages=110–111 }} The FAA hired Frank Briscoe Co. in early 1978 to expand the terminal,{{cite news |date=May 13, 1978 |title=Expansion of Dulles Airport Set to Begin This Summer |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B2 |id={{ProQuest|146916191}} }} and work began that September.{{cite news |last=Morris |first=Wilson |date=September 16, 1978 |title=Building Begins at Duties; East Loading Gates Closed |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C1 |id={{ProQuest|146998226}} }} The same year, the control tower's radome was replaced. The project freed up space in the original terminal for baggage handling, and the FAA awarded a contract to expand the baggage-handling facilities in late 1979.{{cite news |date=November 7, 1979 |title=Airport Improvement Pacts Awarded for National, Dulles |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1979/11/07/airport-improvement-pacts-awarded-for-national-dulles/97b01c31-ed04-4243-a7d7-c2796b349338/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C6 |id={{ProQuest|147236682}} }} HOK's expansion was completed in 1980.{{Cite magazine |last=Freeman |first=Allen |date=Nov 1980 |title=The World's Most Beautiful Airport? |url=https://www.usmodernist.org/AJ/AJ-1980-11.pdf |magazine=Architecture: the AIA Journal |pages=49-50 |volume=69 |issue=13}} By then, customs facilities had been moved to an adjacent temporary structure with four mobile-lounge bays. The expansion came just as patronage at Dulles Airport dropped sharply, in part because of the inconvenience of accessing and using the airport.{{cite news |last=Feaver |first=Douglas B. |date=August 10, 1980 |title=Popularity of National, BWI Brings Hard Times to Dulles |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1980/08/10/popularity-of-national-bwi-brings-hard-times-to-dulles/ad1c1c9e-2efa-46d1-9357-1a9863f4c83a/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=A1 |id={{ProQuest|147080860}} }}{{cite web |last=Hedges |first=Roger |date=December 28, 1980 |title=Dulles Airport: A white elephant eating from U.S. trough |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/battle-creek-enquirer-dulles-airport-a/183189650/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Battle Creek Enquirer |page=30 }} To attract business, the FAA began allowing small planes to load or unload directly at the terminal itself. The FAA rejected plans to add more airline gates to the terminal, citing esthetic concerns and a lack of space.{{cite news |last=Burgess |first=John |date=December 13, 1983 |title=FAA Officials Drafting Plans For 12-Gate Dulles Concourse |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1983/12/13/faa-officials-drafting-plans-for-12-gate-dulles-concourse/2eda09ad-cbdc-40c4-bda2-dfcfd5c3c92f/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C1 |id={{ProQuest|147518909}} }} Instead, in 1983, the agency proposed a "midfield concourse" in the middle of the apron, from which passengers could load onto planes directly.{{cite news |date=November 5, 1983 |title=Concourse, 2 Runways Are Planned for Dulles |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1983/11/05/concourse-2-runways-are-planned-for-dulles/94549cf3-2ea0-48f6-82bd-1f753a9b24e4/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B2 |id={{ProQuest|147569078}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |date=November 5, 1983 |title=New concourse, 2 new runways planned at Dulles |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/daily-press-new-concourse-2-new-runways/183192628/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Daily Press |page=18 }} The first midfield concourse was hastily built and could be accessed only by the mobile lounges.{{cite news |last=Fehr |first=Stephen C. |date=September 8, 1994 |title=Airports Board Backs Dulles Subway Plan |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1994/09/08/airports-board-backs-dulles-subway-plan/da825cda-fc60-4c04-be23-7c52d3cb3ad0/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=A01 |id={{ProQuest|307822918}} }} === Master plan expansion === ==== Mid- and late 1980s ==== In the mid-1980s, as part of a master plan, a consultant recommended doubling the Main Terminal's size, constructing a people-mover to the midfield concourse, and expanding the terminal's airline gates.{{cite news |last=Burgess |first=John |date=April 18, 1984 |title=$197 Million Expansion Suggested for Dulles |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1984/04/18/197-million-expansion-suggested-for-dulles/bc33eca5-ee84-4808-8a84-46f616615908/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C1 |id={{ProQuest|138333658}} }} New vehicular ramps were proposed to alleviate traffic in front of the terminal.{{cite news |last=Henderson |first=Nell |date=November 18, 1987 |title=25-Year-Old Dulles Plans for Tomorrow; Construction to Handle Growth Unveiled at Anniversary Gathering |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1987/11/18/25-year-old-dulles-plans-for-tomorrow/90abc97c-6d39-4919-8f1f-3c7f683da4b9/ |access-date=October 18, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C05 |id={{ProQuest|306947412}} }} The plans also included new facilities for several airlines that used the Main Terminal,{{cite news |date=September 8, 1985 |title=Washington's 'Other' Airport Aims To Triumph Over Its Inconvenience |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |page=52 |id={{ProQuest|111236816}} }}{{Cite magazine |date=March 17, 1986 |title=1985: The Year Dulles Airport Came to Life |magazine=The Business Review |page=22 |volume=11 |issue=11 |id={{ProQuest|197593763}} }} along with a separate terminal for international arrivals.{{Cite magazine |last=Cowan |first=Richard |date=May 1990 |title=Travel Agent: In the Past, Dulles Drew Domestic Businesses to Washington, Now It's Pulling in International Interests |magazine=Regardie's |page=208 |volume=10 |issue=9 |id={{ProQuest|198873778}} }} The expansions came amid rapid growth in the airport's usage, which neared 4{{nbsp}}million by 1984.{{cite news |last=Brown |first=Warren |date=May 13, 1985 |title=Dulles Airport Recovers From White-Elephant Image |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/1985/05/13/dulles-airport-recovers-from-white-elephant-image/d57b1da2-e855-4a88-87b9-586813ce3b12/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |id={{ProQuest|138703324}} |postscript=none}}; {{cite web |last=Gettlin |first=Robert |date=December 15, 1985 |title=Underused in the past, Dulles Airport takes off |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-ann-arbor-news-underused-in-the-past/183193506/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Ann Arbor News |page=F5 }} The master plan was approved by the NCPC in 1986,{{cite news |last=Specter |first=Michael |date=August 1, 1986 |title=Plan Adopted For Expanding Dulles Airport |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1986/08/01/plan-adopted-for-expanding-dulles-airport/ed3fc2e7-f985-430f-9a8d-98e4f5b474bd/ |access-date=October 18, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|139022888}} }} at which point was expected to cost $420{{nbsp}}million.{{Cite magazine |last=Hayden |first=Leslie A. |date=June 9, 1986 |title=Presidential, Pan Am Link, United Expands at Dulles |magazine=The Business Review |page=1 |volume=11 |issue=23 |id={{ProQuest|197630226}} }}{{cite news |last=Henderson |first=Nell |date=May 29, 1987 |title=Less Costly Expansion Of Dulles Airport Urged; Airline Chief Also Backs Multistory Garage |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=D04 |id={{ProQuest|306902843}} }} In the meantime, a clinic, baggage claim areas, and stores in the terminal were added, while the international arrivals area was revamped. The [[Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority]] (MWAA) took over Dulles Airport's operation in 1987 and assumed responsibility for the expansion program.{{cite web |date=June 6, 1987 |title=National, Dulles airports slated for work |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-national-dulles/183197491/ |access-date=October 18, 2025 |website=Richmond Times-Dispatch |page=8 }} [[David Childs]] and Marilyn Taylor of [[Skidmore, Owings & Merrill]] (SOM) were hired to design a master plan for the terminal, which was rapidly approaching its annual capacity of 13{{nbsp}}million passengers. Jr. |date=August 6, 1988 |title=Employees Turn On No-Smoking Signs at Dulles Airport |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1988/08/06/employees-turn-on-no-smoking-signs-at-dulles-airport/2a3fe932-ad70-4a25-87e2-0fcbc4dcb422/ |access-date=October 18, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B07 |id={{ProQuest|307072713}} }} The same year, to alleviate congestion at the Main Terminal, the MWAA began constructing the international arrivals terminal,{{cite news |date=June 24, 1988 |title=1st Airport Contract |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=C07 |id={{ProQuest|307041769}} }} which was designed by SOM to the west of the original terminal. Paul J. C. Friedlander, of ''[[The New York Times]]'', said the swooping roof and slanted glass facade created an effect of "grace and lightness". The commentator Walter McQuade wrote for ''[[Architectural Forum]]'': "It is likely that the most majestic single statement of this integrated expressionism will be his design for Dulles Terminal."{{harvnb|McQuade|1962|page=107|ps=. }} Saarinen had deemed the Dulles Main Terminal "the best thing I have done"; of the projects he had been working on when he died, he had been especially proud of the Dulles terminal and New York's [[CBS Building]].{{cite magazine |last=Larrabee |first=Eric |date=December 1, 1964 |title=Saarinen's Dark Tower |url=https://harpers.org/archive/1964/12/saarinens-dark-tower/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716200146/https://harpers.org/archive/1964/12/saarinens-dark-tower/ |archive-date=July 16, 2021 |access-date=July 15, 2021 |magazine=Harper's Magazine |page=55 |volume=229 |issue=1375 |id={{ProQuest|1301532669}} }} Saarinen's wife, the architectural critic [[Aline B. Saarinen]], similarly believed the terminal would be her husband's "best work".{{cite web |last=Lensing |first=Mildred |date=February 15, 1962 |title=Mrs. Eero Saarinen Continues to Build Her Husband's Work |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-courier-journal-mrs-eero-saarinen-c/183115985/ |access-date=October 16, 2025 |website=The Courier-Journal |page=13 }} Although the [[Associated Press]] wrote that the completed terminal "was too modern for many tastes when it was built", the [[Architectural Record|''Architectural Record'']] said the building "was almost instantly regarded as a Modern masterpiece". When the terminal opened, ''[[Newsday]]'' of New York described the building as "definitely a design of the future", and a reporter for the ''Baltimore Sun'' said the structure "looks better the closer one gets to it", ''Architectural Forum'', in a 1963 article, wrote that the terminal "happily will never grow into an octopus", referring to the lack of jetways.{{harvnb|Architectural Forum|1963|ps=.|page=72 }} The [[Associated Press]] wrote that the walls, interior lighting, and control tower combined to create "a dreamlike appearance" at night. The architect [[Cesar Pelli]], a former employee of Saarinen's, described the feeling of approaching the Dulles terminal as being similar to that of approaching a "great temple or a great cathedral in the countryside in France". terminal's beauty, saying: "The trouble is, Mr. Saarinen forgot to put in the engines."{{cite web |last=Howe |first=Dan |date=February 26, 1963 |title=Dulles Airport Is 'Way Out' |via=newspapers.com terminal, along with [[Boston City Hall]], as "the greatest [building] on the American scene in a decade or two".{{cite news |last=Von Eckardt |first=Wolf |date=April 2, 1967 |title=Boston Builds Challenge to Dulles Terminal: An Excellent Plan The Obscure Winners A Tide Into City Hall |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=C3 |id={{ProQuest|143202830}} }} Conversely, [[Morris Lapidus]] wrote for [[Architecture: The AIA Journal|''Architecture: The AIA Journal'']] in 1964 that, although the building's exterior was "beautifully bold and daring", the interior lacked scale or embellishing details.{{cite magazine |last=Lapidus |first=Morris |date=Feb 1964 |title=A Quest for {{Not a typo|Living|space}} In Architecture |url=https://www.usmodernist.org/AJ/AJ-1964-02.pdf |magazine=Architecture: the AIA Journal |page=38 |volume=XLI |issue=2 }} ==== Retrospective ==== Retrospectively, a commentator for the ''[[Reporter-Times]]'' described early reactions as negative, saying that the local and state governments had only reluctantly accepted Saarinen's design.{{Cite news |last=Finkelstein |first=Lydia |date=January 11, 2004 |title=Amazing achievements of the 20th century |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-reporter-times-amazing-achievements/172573622/ |access-date=May 17, 2025 |work=The Reporter-Times |pages=46 }} A ''New York Times'' article, conversely, characterized the building as having been perceived "as a bold reflection of American aviation" from the outset.{{cite web |last=Dorman |first=John L. |date=October 6, 2017 |title=Eero Saarinen's Michigan |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/06/travel/eero-saarinen-michigan-architecture-modernist-design.html |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} In 1977, when the terminal's expansion was first being considered, a ''Washington Post'' writer deemed the terminal Dulles Airport's "one great strength", saying it "looks far more capable of flight" than ordinary aircraft. Upon the terminal's 20th anniversary in 1982, ''The New York Times'' wrote that it was "considered by many to be a landmark of 20th-century design".{{cite web |date=July 16, 1982 |title=Dulles Airport Still Waits for Traffic |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/07/16/us/dulles-airport-still-waits-for-traffic.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} ''The Washington Post'' referred to the terminal in 1989 as "inspiring from afar and maddening from within" because of the overcrowding inside.{{cite news |last=Henderson |first=Nell |date=November 1, 1989 |title=Airport Eyes Prominent Architect |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1989/11/01/airport-eyes-prominent-architect/52cc9763-1ce9-48da-a647-dc00428993bd/ |access-date=October 19, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 |page=B01 |id={{ProQuest|307242980}} }} A writer for [[The Wilson Quarterly|''The Wilson Quarterly'']] wrote in 1995 that the Dulles Main Terminal and the [[TWA Flight Center]] demonstrated how Saarinen "push[ed] design beyond the confines of the Modern Movement".{{Cite magazine |last=Rybczynski |first=Witold |date=Spring 1995 |title=Farewell to modernism – The Oral History of Modern Architecture: Interviews with the Greatest Architects of the Twentieth Century by John Peter |magazine=The Wilson Quarterly |page=80 |volume=19 |issue=2 |id={{ProQuest|197240934}} }} A writer for ''The New York Times'' said in 2003 that the Dulles Airport Main Terminal, like Saarinen's nearly-contemporary [[North Christian Church]], "immediately seizes even the casual onlooker's eye with its dramatic shape and carries it heavenward".{{cite web |last=Apple |first=R. W. Jr. |date=December 5, 2003 |title=HAVENS; A Farmland Showcase For Modern Architecture |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/05/travel/havens-a-farmland-showcase-for-modern-architecture.html |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} The next year, the writer Mark Gottdiener praised the exterior as a "dramatic, austere statement" but said that the interior, particularly the inefficiency of the mobile lounges, was inadequate. A 2006 book about Saarinen's architecture said that his design "gave structure an expressive dimension".{{harvnb|Pelkonen|Albrecht|2006|page=1|ps=. }} Roger K. Lewis wrote in 2010 that the terminal had aged well over the years, not only because the interiors were so easily adaptable to different uses, but also because the terminal's design was simple yet memorable.{{cite news |last=Lewis |first=Roger K. |date=December 4, 2010 |title=Architect's legacy soars at Dulles Airport |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/realestate/2010/12/04/architects-legacy-soars-at-dulles-airport/9017895a-fe9e-11df-acb2-d71d2f79858f/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 }} Over the years, the building's design has also evoked comparisons to birds.{{cite news |last=Aratani |first=Lori |date=November 22, 2012 |title=Dulles Airport celebrates 50th anniversary |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/local/trafficandcommuting/dulles-airport-celebrates-50th-anniversary/2012/11/22/675f926a-33f2-11e2-9cfa-e41bac906cc9_story.html |access-date=October 20, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 }} {{Wide image|Panorama of Dulles Airport, Virginia LCCN2011634458.tif|600px|View of the terminal at dusk}} === Awards and architectural influence === The [[Greater Washington Board of Trade]] gave the terminal building an award for its design in 1964,{{cite news |last=Lescaze |first=Lee |date=September 11, 1964 |title=13 Area Buildings Lauded for Design: News Analysis |work=The Washington Post, Times Herald |issn=0190-8286 |page=B1 |id={{ProQuest|142163932}} }} and Saarinen's firm received an honor award from the [[American Institute of Architects]] (AIA) in 1966 for the terminal's design.{{cite web |date=July 3, 1966 |title=Architects Pick Award-winning Building Designs; Institute of Architects Presents Honor Awards for 12 Buildings |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1966/07/03/archives/architects-pick-awardwinning-building-designs-institute-of.html |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }}{{cite web |date=July 10, 1966 |title=Judged Best in American Architecture |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-star-judged-best-in-amer/183173233/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=The Kansas City Star |page=69 }} A 1976 poll of American architects ranked it the country's third-best design, tied with [[Fallingwater]],{{cite news |last=Gapp |first=Paul |date=July 26, 1976 |title=Jefferson building best design in 200 years: Architects name 'proudest achievements' Jefferson's rotunda tops list |work=Chicago Tribune |page=5 |issn=1085-6706 |id={{ProQuest|169443866}} }} and one of the most impactful buildings constructed in the U.S. since the [[American Revolution]]. The Dulles Main Terminal won the AIA's [[Twenty-five Year Award]] in 1988. The [[United States Postal Service]] issued a stamp depicting the terminal in 1982 to honor Saarinen's designs,{{cite web |last=Tower |first=Samuel A. |date=September 26, 1982 |title=Stamps; Honoring Four Great American Architects |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1982/09/26/arts/stamps-honoring-four-great-american-architects.html |access-date=August 22, 2025 |website=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 }} and the terminal was also included in the 2013 [[PBS]] documentary and companion book ''[[10 That Changed America|10 Buildings that Changed America]]''.{{cite web |last=Webb |first=Tom |date=June 24, 2012 |title=Southdale Center named among nation's 10 most influential buildings |url=https://www.twincities.com/2012/06/24/southdale-center-named-among-nations-10-most-influential-buildings/ |access-date=October 20, 2025 |website=Twin Cities}} * For the list of buildings, see: {{cite web |date=February 27, 2016 |title=10 Buildings that Changed America |url=https://www.wttw.com/ten/buildings |access-date=February 7, 2025 |website=WTTW Chicago }} When the terminal was first expanded in the 1970s, there were calls for the Dulles Main Terminal to be added to the [[National Register of Historic Places]] (NRHP).{{cite web |last=Gapp |first=Paul |date=March 26, 1978 |title=Preservation lands at Dulles Airport |via=newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/chicago-tribune-preservation-lands-at-du/183181160/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |website=Chicago Tribune |page=129 }} This would have made it one of the youngest-ever NRHP listings, as most NRHP sites cannot be listed until they are at least fifty years old. The FAA opposed the NRHP designation, as it would have subjected any potential renovations to a lengthy approval process. The terminal was deemed eligible for NRHP listing in 1978, on the merits of its design.{{cite news |last=Hodge |first=Paul |date=February 23, 1978 |title=Dulles Nominated To Historic List To Protect Design |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1978/02/23/dulles-nominated-to-historic-list-to-protect-design/8f36f69b-6230-435f-96e5-59d9e82b78f1/ |access-date=October 17, 2025 |newspaper=The Washington Post |issn=0190-8286 }} Ultimately, it was never added to the NRHP because of the FAA's concerns that such a designation would disrupt airport operations.{{cite news
